tier_reason: First-party numbers: benchmarks/results.json (merged from benchmarks/results_cpp.json) holds every per-feature figure and the 541.45 ms vs 38949.54 ms full-pipeline figure exactly as claimed, produced by public code (benchmarks/bench_cpp.cpp for the C++ side, benchmarks/run_bench.py for librosa 0.11.0 pinned in benchmarks/pyproject.toml). benchmarks/README.md names the Apple M5 Max as the published reference machine and gives the Release cmake line, but no compiler or compiler version is stated, so not A.

corrections.hardware: Apple M5 Max (benchmarks/README.md: 'M5 Max numbers are the published reference'); results record 18 hardware threads; load average 2.29/2.43 during the C++ run (results_cpp.json) and 2.49/3.09 during the librosa run (results.json)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: CMake Release build (cmake -B build-bench -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DBUILD_BENCH=ON -DBUILD_TESTING=OFF -DBUILD_CLI=OFF); the root CMakeLists.txt adds no optimization or -march flags beyond the Release defaults; PFFFT SIMD FFT backend on by default; compiler and version not stated
corrections.workload: Per-feature timing from raw audio (every call rebuilds STFT/Mel from samples) on a deterministic synthetic 73 s 44.1 kHz stereo fixture, downmixed and resampled to 22.05 kHz outside the timed region (librosa.load on the Python side, sonare::resample on the C++ side); median of 3 runs per case, no warmup; C++ timed with chrono::steady_clock inside sonare_bench, librosa with time.perf_counter around each call using librosa defaults (n_fft 2048, hop 512). Plus the full analyze() pipeline versus the same author's librosa-based bpm-detector 1.1.0 --comprehensive run as a subprocess.
corrections.caveats: Authors' own benchmark: public scripts and a named CPU (Apple M5 Max) but no compiler, so tier C. Baseline is a Python library; the biggest gaps (HPSS 26.64x, pYIN 15.77x) come from libsonare's threaded paths using every core against mostly single-threaded librosa, and benchmarks/README.md says the WASM build is single-threaded and these speedups shrink there. The 71.94x full-pipeline figure compares against bpm-detector (the same author's earlier librosa-based program, timed as a subprocess including Python start-up and imports), not librosa itself. Beat tracking is slower than librosa (0.78x). Inputs are resampled by different resamplers on each side, so the two libraries do not see byte-identical samples. Synthetic fixture only. Audio analysis, not a codec, so it is off the FFmpeg/x264/Opus category baselines.

notes: All claimed numbers match results.json exactly; harness reads like-for-like per feature (both sides standalone from raw audio, median of 3). Hardware is stated after all (M5 Max in benchmarks/README.md), but compiler is not, so C stands; keep with the off-baseline shortcoming.

tier_reason: First-party numbers from a public script, scripts/performance_benchmark.py, which produced images/execution_time_comparison.png (chart title 'Execution times for 5 minutes of mono 48 kHz audio'); the five timings match the README alt text. No CPU, compiler or flags are stated and each library is timed once with time.time(), so C.

corrections.workload: Integrated loudness (LUFS) of 5 minutes of mono 48 kHz float32 uniform white noise (np.random.uniform, 14.4M samples) held in a NumPy array; one timed call per library with time.time(), no warmup or repetition. loudness uses Meter<EBU_I|Histogram>.addFrames (single-threaded path); pyebur128 uses R128State MODE_I add_frames; the pyloudness timing includes writing and reading a temporary WAV file.
corrections.claimed_speedup: Execution time for 5 minutes of mono 48 kHz audio: loudness 0.1.0 0.056 s; pyebur128 0.1.1 0.096 s; torchaudio 2.8.0 0.282 s; pyloudnorm 0.1.1 0.293 s; pyloudness 1.1.2 0.581 s. About 1.7x over pyebur128 (libebur128 via Cython), 5.0x over torchaudio, 5.2x over pyloudnorm, 10.4x over pyloudness (derived from page data). README: 'significantly faster than the alternatives when running on CPU'.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated; built with scikit-build-core (default Release) and CMake, C++20, no extra optimization flags in CMakeLists.txt; published wheels come from cibuildwheel
corrections.caveats: Numbers come from one run per library timed with time.time() on synthetic white noise, with no CPU, compiler or OS stated; the chart was made with loudness 0.1.0 (current release 0.2.0). The closest baseline, pyebur128 (a Cython wrapper of libebur128), is only about 1.7x slower; the larger ratios are against pure-Python or torch implementations, and the pyloudness time includes WAV file I/O. The C++ core is Nomono's libloudness (MIT, described upstream as a C++ port of libebur128 with optimizations), compiled into this Python package; use from C++ means vendoring src/loudness. Off the category's FFmpeg/x264/Opus baselines (audio loudness metering).

notes: The record said no audio length or script was given; both exist (scripts/performance_benchmark.py, chart title gives 5 min mono 48 kHz). Single-shot timings make the 1.7x over pyebur128 noisy but not invalid. Upstream nomonosound/libloudness (10 stars, MIT) carries no numbers of its own and is not in the catalog, so no duplicate.

tier_reason: First-party numbers from a public harness (tests/comprehensive_bench.py, tests/bench_thread_modes.py, tests/utils/bench_harness.py) with checked-in results (tests/output/comprehensive/final/results.json, tests/output/thread_modes.json) and a named CPU (i9-13900K), but no compiler version or flags for the benchmarked wheel, so C. The claim is overstated: the decode is FFmpeg's libavcodec in every row, and the margins over the ffmpeg CLI come from parallel libswscale conversion and from the baseline paying process start-up per run.

corrections.claimed_speedup: From tests/output/comprehensive/final/results.json (Windows 11, i9-13900K + RTX 3090), fps for H.264 decode to RGB uint8: default reader (prefetch=False, 'nelux-cpu-sync') 3393.5 / 2563.4 / 539.4 at 720p / 1080p / 4K; prefetch row ('nelux-cpu-fanout', which the README headline labels 'nelux (default)') 3422 / 2642 / 607; torchcodec 2924 / 1589 / 367; ffmpeg CLI -vf format=rgb24 subprocess 2273 / 1102 / 254; ffmpeg decode-only -f null subprocess 2906 / 2638 / 735. Default reader over ffmpeg-rgb24: 1.49x / 2.33x / 2.13x; over torchcodec: 1.16x / 1.61x / 1.47x (derived from page data). With convert_workers=0 (tests/output/thread_modes.json): 3167 vs torchcodec 3090 at 720p, 1755 vs 1728 at 1080p, 394 vs 401 at 4K, i.e. parity. NVDEC fps nelux vs ffmpeg -hwaccel cuda -f null subprocess: 1651 vs 1253, 667 vs 592, 175 vs 162 (1.32x / 1.13x / 1.08x, derived from page data).
corrections.workload: H.264 decode to RGB uint8 HWC tensors: 720p Big Buck Bunny clip and synthetic 1080p and 4K H.264 clips, 600 frames per run (300 at 4K). nelux and torchcodec are timed in-process after the reader is constructed; the ffmpeg baselines are CLI subprocesses (-vf format=rgb24 -f rawvideo to the null device for CPU; -hwaccel cuda -hwaccel_output_format cuda -f null for NVDEC, which does no RGB conversion) timed including process launch, probe and decoder/CUDA initialisation. The published final/results.json rows are single records (about 0.18-0.6 s of wall time, one resource sample each), not the medians the README describes.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Compiler version and flags of the benchmarked wheel not stated. Current CMakeLists.txt forces Release with LTO and fast-math on and AVX2 off; README says Windows builds need MSVC 18; build via scikit-build-core + CMake + Ninja + vcpkg. Decode work is FFmpeg's libavcodec (README: FFmpeg 8.x at benchmark time; wheels now pin TAS-FFMPEG 8.1.2 in tools/ffmpeg.lock). The ffmpeg CLI baseline is whatever ffmpeg is on PATH (shutil.which); tests/output/perf_findings.md names ffmpeg 8.0.1-gyan on the test machine. Results file records nelux_version 0.10.1 while the README says 0.11.0.
corrections.caveats: Decoding is FFmpeg's libavcodec (software H.264 with frame threads, and FFmpeg's CUDA path for NVDEC), so none of the gain is codec speed. The README itself says the win over torchcodec is entirely the convert worker pool: with convert_workers=0 nelux is within about 2% of torchcodec, and the default fan-out costs about 2.5-3x the CPU (874-1656% vs 344-502%). The ffmpeg baselines are CLI subprocesses timed including process start-up, probe and decoder init, while nelux is timed after reader construction; at 720p the ffmpeg decode-only run (-f null, no RGB conversion) reaches only 2906 fps against nelux's 3394 fps with conversion, which shows the fixed per-process cost in the baseline. The NVDEC baseline does no NV12-to-RGB conversion and its gap shrinks from 32% at 720p to 8% at 4K as per-run time grows, the pattern of amortised start-up rather than faster decode. The README headline row labelled 'nelux (default)' matches the prefetch ('nelux-cpu-fanout') row in final/results.json; the prefetch=False default row is 3393.5 / 2563.4 / 539.4 fps. Published rows are single short runs (about 0.18 s at 720p) without stored medians, measured on nelux 0.10.1/0.11.0; the decode path has changed since (0.16.0-0.20.0). Single hardware data point on Windows 11. AGPL-3.0.

notes: Not a thin binding (own threaded convert pool and fused CUDA NV12-to-RGB kernel over FFmpeg), so not marked duplicate, but its speed claim over FFmpeg is pipeline and threading, not decoding; the orchestrator may still prefer folding it under the FFmpeg entry. Numbers are real (they match checked-in result files); the overstatement is the 'default' label and the start-up-handicapped subprocess baseline.
